options.label: Progress. We stopped policing bedrooms.
Decline. We stopped expecting character.

facts: Gary Hart, the Democratic front-runner for 1988, suspended his campaign on May 8, 1987, days after the Miami Herald reported on his relationship with Donna Rice.

prompt: Should each of these end a political career? Yes or no, four seconds each.

cards.text: An affair twenty years ago should end a career.
An affair with someone who reports to them should end a career.
A divorce in the middle of the campaign should end a career.
Private photos leaked by a bitter ex should end a career.
A third marriage should end a career.
Campaign money spent keeping a story quiet should end a career.
Lying about it under oath should end a career.

prompt: Power is attractive. Anyone who has worked a campaign knows the candidate gets looked at differently by month three. What follows from that?

options.label: True, and harmless when adults behave like adults.
True, and exactly why the rules should be strict.
True, and half the reason anyone runs.
Overrated. The job is mostly committee meetings.

prompt: An unsigned note under your door: your campaign manager and your communications director are sleeping together. Both are single. Both are essential. What do you do with the note?

options.label: Toss the note. Two adults, their own time.
They tell counsel, and one stops reporting to the other.
One of them has to go. Pick by Friday.

artNote: A hotel room doorway at night seen from inside: a folded sheet of hotel notepaper half under the door, a strip of corridor light. On the desk behind, two lanyards and two coffee cups. No people.

prompt: The story about your marriage broke this morning. The press conference is in five minutes. Where should your spouse be?

regions.label: Beside the podium — next to me, holding my hand
regions.where: center, the space right next to the podium

regions.label: By the flags — a step behind me, eyes on the floor
regions.where: center back, in front of the flags

regions.label: The front row — among the press, their own choice of seat
regions.where: bottom left, the first row of folding chairs

regions.label: The television — at home. They are not a prop.
regions.where: top right, a television in the corner showing a quiet house

regions.label: The podium — they speak instead of me
regions.where: center, the podium microphones themselves

artNote: An empty press room minutes before a statement: podium with microphones at center, flags behind, rows of folding chairs filling the foreground, a wall television at top right showing a still shot of a suburban house. No people are drawn; regions are the empty places a person would stand.

prompt: A candidate and their spouse have, by every account, an arrangement. They are discreet and they are happy. A reporter has the story. Should it run?

options.label: Voters are choosing a person. They should know.
Nobody's business. Spike it.

prompt: What do you make of a politician with thirty years in public life and not one scandal?

slider.centre: Careful, which is not the same as clean

prompt: Your party's values voters have backed a nominee whose private life they would once have ruled out. Looking back, what was that?

options.label: Right. Judge the judges he picked, not the marriages.
A bargain that cost us our standing to talk about character.
Grace. Everyone falls short; forgiveness is the point.
Proof that character is graded on a curve, and winners set it.

facts: Donald Trump, three times married, won the Republican nomination in 2016, 2020 and 2024; the Access Hollywood tape was published on October 7, 2016. Mike Pence declined to endorse him in March 2024.

prompt: In 1998 your party defended a president through an affair with a White House intern. Twenty years on, some of its own senators said he should have resigned. Who was right?

options.label: 1998. Private conduct, political prosecution.
The rethink. The power gap was the whole point.
He should have gone at the time.
Right politics, wrong morals. We would do it again.

facts: Bill Clinton was impeached by the House on December 19, 1998 and acquitted by the Senate on February 12, 1999. In November 2017 Senator Kirsten Gillibrand said he should have resigned.

prompt: A tabloid editor offers you proof of your rival's affair. He wants nothing for it. Yet. What do you do with it?

options.label: Decline. Their marriage is not my campaign.
options.receipt: A tabloid offered you proof of your rival's affair. You declined it.

options.label: Let it surface somewhere with no trail back to me.
options.receipt: Handed proof of your rival's affair, you let it surface with no trail back to you.

options.label: Use it openly. He ran on family values.
options.receipt: Handed proof of your rival's affair, you used it in the open.

options.label: Let the rival know I have it. Then say nothing.
options.receipt: You let your rival know you had the proof of his affair, and then you said nothing at all.

prompt: Your communications director closes the door and confesses: for six months she has been seeing the reporter who covers your campaign. Her resignation letter is on your desk. Do you accept it?

options.label: Accept it. The coverage is tainted either way.
Refuse it. Tell the reporter's editor and move on.
Put the letter in a drawer. Ask what the reporter knows.

artNote: A campaign office with the blinds drawn. An invented woman in her thirties in a blazer stands with her back against the closed door. On the desk, a single typed letter, unsigned, and a press pass that is not hers.

prompt: A candidate is 45, single, and dating openly during the campaign. What do you think?

options.label: Good for them. Presidents are allowed a Friday night.
Fine. Just keep it off the feed.
Voters want a settled family in that house.
Get engaged before the first primary votes. It polls.

prompt: The man who made your career asks you for one thing. You have read the law and you believe the Constitution does not let you do it. What do you do?

options.label: Do it. I am here because of him.
options.receipt: The man who made your career asked for something the Constitution forbids. You did it.

options.label: Say no in writing, then do my duty.
options.receipt: Your patron asked for something unlawful. You refused him in writing.

options.label: Say no quietly and get on with governing.
Find a reason to be out of the room.
options.receipt: Your patron asked you to break the law. You found a reason to be out of the room.

facts: On January 6, 2021 Mike Pence released a letter saying he had no authority to reject electoral votes, and presided over certification. In late 2020 Brian Kemp declined President Trump's requests to call a special session to overturn Georgia's result.

prompt: Eight years ago he humiliated you on a debate stage. Now he hands out the jobs, and he is offering you one. Do you take it?

options.label: Take it and serve him without a flicker.
Endorse him, keep my own microphone.
Help him win. Turn on him the day it sours.
No. Some things you do not come back from.

facts: Donald Trump mocked Marco Rubio as Little Marco in 2016; Rubio was confirmed as his Secretary of State 99-0 on January 20, 2025. Trump attacked Ted Cruz's wife and father in 2016; Cruz endorsed him on September 23, 2016. Chris Christie endorsed Trump on February 26, 2016 and ran against him from June 6, 2023.

prompt: Your party's president is visibly slowing down. The election is a year away. You sit in his cabinet and you have seen it up close. What do you do?

options.label: Stand by him in public. That is the job.
Tell him to his face, alone, and tell no one else.
Let a reporter know what people are saying.
Say it on the record, first, and take the hit.

facts: Joe Biden withdrew from the 2024 race on July 21, 2024, after his June 27 debate. Vice President Kamala Harris defended him publicly until he withdrew; on The View on October 8, 2024, asked what she would have done differently from him, she said nothing came to mind.

prompt: An unfair attack on you lands at 9 a.m. What have you done by noon?

slider.centre: Answered it once and moved on

facts: Gavin Newsom's press office spent August 2025 answering President Trump with all-caps parody posts. Andy Beshear has built his brand on avoiding partisan name-calling.

prompt: Picture it: you have lost the primary. The winner called you a fraud on live television in March. Their people are on the phone asking for your endorsement. Do you give it?

options.label: Endorse this week. The party comes first.
Not yet. Let them come to me, and bring something.

facts: Pete Buttigieg left the 2020 race on March 1, 2020 and endorsed Joe Biden in Dallas on March 2, 2020, the day before Super Tuesday. Ron DeSantis left the 2024 race and endorsed Donald Trump on January 21, 2024.

prompt: A courier from your party leader's office: a statement attacking a colleague, with a line for your signature. The colleague is your friend. They want it back by noon. Do you sign?

options.label: Sign it.
options.receipt: The leader sent a statement attacking your friend. You signed it by noon.

options.label: Rewrite it softer, sign that, and hope.
options.receipt: Asked to sign an attack on your friend, you softened the wording and signed that.

options.label: Send it back unsigned. No covering note.
options.receipt: They wanted your name on an attack on a friend. You sent it back unsigned.

artNote: A senator's desk at midday: a single typed page with a blank signature line, a fountain pen uncapped beside it, a wall clock showing ten to twelve. A courier, invented, waits in the doorway with a satchel, seen from behind.

prompt: Your party's signature bill is on the floor. You think it is a bad bill. The leader needs every vote and has said so by name. How do you vote?

options.label: Vote no and say exactly why.
Object loudly in print, then vote yes.
Vote yes. You do not sink your own team.
Sell the vote for something my state needs.

facts: The Senate passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act 51-50 on July 1, 2025, with Vice President Vance breaking the tie; Rand Paul voted no. Josh Hawley criticized its Medicaid cuts in a New York Times essay in May 2025 and voted yes.

prompt: A member of the other party offers to co-sponsor something your voters want and your leadership hates. Do you take the offer?

options.label: Do it, loudly, and dare leadership to stop me.
Do it quietly. Results, not headlines.
Ask leadership first.
Decline. You do not hand the other side a win.

facts: In 2025 Ro Khanna, a Democrat, and Republican Thomas Massie led a discharge petition to force a House vote on releasing the Epstein files; the House passed the measure on November 18, 2025.

prompt: Fight or fold? Would you do it: yes or no, four seconds each.

cards.text: Answer a heckler from the podium.
Give your opponent a nickname.
Apologize, in public, when you got it wrong.
Sue a newspaper.
Shake hands warmly after a brutal debate.
Post a reply at 1 a.m.
Keep a list of who crossed you.

prompt: The network your base cannot stand invites you on for a full hour, live, with their toughest host. Do you go?

options.label: Go, and win the argument on their turf.
Better: invite their stars onto my own show.
Refuse. You do not lend them your credibility.
Go, and be so pleasant they have nothing to clip.

facts: Pete Buttigieg has made regular appearances on Fox News since 2019. Gavin Newsom launched a podcast in March 2025 whose early guests included Charlie Kirk and Steve Bannon.

prompt: The party's most polarizing figure offers to fly in and rally for you in the suburbs you need. His base loves him. The suburbs do not. Do you share the stage?

options.label: On stage together, arms raised.
Thank him warmly. Plead a scheduling conflict.

facts: In the 2021 Virginia governor's race Glenn Youngkin accepted Donald Trump's endorsement but never appeared with him in person; Trump held a telephone rally on November 1, 2021 that Youngkin did not join.

prompt: In politics, who is loyalty owed to?

slider.left: To principles. People come and go.
slider.right: To the person who made you.
slider.centre: To the party that carries both

prompt: Years ago you called your party's leader unfit for office. It is on tape. Now he is offering you a place on the ticket. What do you do?

options.label: I was wrong and he proved it. Say so, often.
options.receipt: You once called him unfit, on tape. Offered the ticket, you said you had been wrong, and said it often.

options.label: I meant it then and I mean it now. Decline.
options.receipt: Offered a place on the ticket by a man you once called unfit, you said you still meant it.

options.label: Different time. Never discuss it again.
Accept. Keep my own copy of the tape.
options.receipt: You once called your party's leader unfit, on tape. When he offered you the ticket you accepted, and kept your own copy of the tape.

facts: In 2016 JD Vance described himself as a Never Trump guy and criticized Donald Trump in interviews and print; he later said he had been wrong, and Trump named him running mate on July 15, 2024.

prompt: You won. Rank who you owe, most to least.

options.label: The leader who made me
The party
The donors
The voters
My own conscience

prompt: The nominee's lawyers are vetting you for vice president. The last page of the questionnaire has one line: Would you ever disagree with the nominee in public? What do you write?

options.label: Write: Never.
options.receipt: The vetting form asked if you would ever disagree with the nominee in public. You wrote: Never.

options.label: Write: Only behind a closed door.
options.receipt: Asked if you would ever disagree with the nominee, you wrote: only behind a closed door.

options.label: Write: Yes, when it matters. You should want that.
options.receipt: Asked in writing if you would ever contradict the nominee, you wrote yes.

artNote: A law-firm conference room, blinds half closed. A thick vetting questionnaire open at its last page with one printed question and a blank line; a pen laid across it. Two invented lawyers in gray suits sit opposite, out of focus.

prompt: A Republican legislature will pass your roads and bridges bill tomorrow, if you give them the school voucher program your own base hates. Do you take the deal?

options.label: Take the deal. Governing is getting things built.
No deal. You do not trade away your own side.

facts: Scenario invented. Josh Shapiro spoke favorably of Lifeline Scholarships (private-school vouchers) while campaigning in 2022 and backed a $100 million voucher program (renamed PASS) in the 2023 budget talks; on July 5, 2023 he said he would line-item veto it to end the impasse with House Democrats, and did so when he signed the budget on August 3, 2023.

prompt: The back room, after midnight. The nomination is not settled and everything you need is on the table. What is your next move?

regions.label: The sealed folder — use the dirt on my rival
regions.where: left third of the table, a thick folder tied with red string

regions.label: The phone — call the party boss
regions.where: center of the table, an old desk telephone

regions.label: The decanter — pour one for the other side and deal
regions.where: right third of the table, a cut-glass decanter and two glasses

regions.label: The mirror — check how I look
regions.where: back wall, top center, a tarnished gilt mirror

regions.label: The door — leave. None of this is for me.
regions.where: far right, a heavy door standing slightly open

artNote: A smoke-stained private room, one hanging lamp over a round table. On the table, left to right: a folder tied with red string, an old desk telephone, a cut-glass decanter with two glasses. A tarnished gilt mirror on the back wall, a heavy door ajar at far right. No people.

prompt: Your campaign war chest is 100 points. How do you spend it?

options.label: Warm ads about me
Attack ads
Opposition research
Pay and health coverage for field staff
Relatives on the payroll as advisers

prompt: You won. One hundred appointments to hand out. Who gets them?

options.label: Loyalists who were there from the start
The best experts, whoever they backed
Donors
Family
Beaten rivals, to keep them close

prompt: The scandal breaks at 9 p.m. You have 100 minutes before the late news. How do you spend them?

options.label: With the lawyers
With my spouse
On cable, denying everything
Finding out who leaked
Writing a real apology

prompt: The president's political office sends every hopeful the same envelope: a pledge to back whoever he names as successor, before a single vote. Sign, or lose his donor list. Do you sign?

options.label: Sign it and post a photo of the signature.
Lose the envelope. Praise him on television instead.
Tear it up on stage.

artNote: A campaign bus table at night: a heavy cream envelope, opened, with a one-page pledge and a blank signature line. A marker pen beside it. Out of the window, the lights of a rally site. No real seals or names on the paper.
facts: Scenario; no such pledge is on the record.

prompt: A tech billionaire's fixer leaves an offer in your hotel room: $50 million to an outside group backing you. One unwritten condition: you go quiet on breaking up his industry. What do you do?

options.label: Take it. I can do more good in office than out.
options.receipt: A billionaire offered fifty million for your silence. You took it and called it doing good.

options.label: Post a photo of it. Name him.
options.receipt: A billionaire's fixer left fifty million in your hotel room. You posted a photo and named him.

options.label: Take the meeting, promise nothing, let the money land.
options.receipt: Offered fifty million to go quiet, you promised nothing and let the money land.

artNote: A hotel room desk: a slim folder with a two-page term sheet, figures blurred, held shut by a plain paperclip, left square on the blotter beside the room key. City lights through the window. No people, no company logos.
facts: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has refused corporate PAC money since her 2018 campaign.

prompt: A colleague in your own caucus has made a fortune trading stocks, with timing that looks a lot like committee knowledge. Leadership would like everyone to keep quiet. What do you do?

options.label: Push a trading ban for all of us, and say why now.
A quiet word with the colleague.
Keep quiet. You do not shoot inside the tent.
Find out what they bought.

facts: Jon Ossoff and Mark Kelly introduced the Ban Congressional Stock Trading Act on January 12, 2022. Josh Hawley introduced his own ban, the PELOSI Act, in January 2023 and reintroduced it in April 2025; a revised version, the HONEST Act, cleared a Senate committee on July 30, 2025.

prompt: A serving general tells you privately he has been given an order he believes is unlawful. He asks what you are prepared to say in public. What do you do?

options.label: Say it to camera: no one has to obey an illegal order.
options.receipt: A general told you he had been given an unlawful order. You said so to a camera.

options.label: Take it to the committees and the inspectors.
Stay out. The chain of command is not mine to break.
options.receipt: A general brought you an unlawful order. You decided the chain of command was not your business.

options.label: Hold it for October. It will hit harder.
options.receipt: A general told you about an unlawful order. You saved it for October.

facts: On November 18, 2025 Elissa Slotkin, Mark Kelly and four other Democratic lawmakers with military or intelligence backgrounds released a video telling service members they can refuse illegal orders; President Trump called it seditious behavior and on November 24, 2025 the Pentagon announced a review of Kelly.

prompt: The leader's endorsement made you a governor. Six years on, the polls say you could beat him. What do you do?

options.label: Run against him. Gratitude is not a term limit.
Wait. Be the obvious choice when he is gone.
Ask for his blessing and run as his heir.
Run, but never say his name.

facts: Donald Trump endorsed Ron DeSantis for governor of Florida in 2018; DeSantis announced his run against Trump for the 2024 nomination on May 24, 2023.
